newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PRESS DIGEST - HK newspaper headlines - Oct 9.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - HK newspaper headlines - Oct 9.

text.p: These are some of the leading stories in the Hong Kong press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
-- WEN WEI PO - Beijing denounced the behaviour of Japanese illegal right-wing groups and urged the Japanese government to ban them.
-- MING PAO - According to a member of the Preparatory Committee, Hong Kong chief executive candidates who gave up their British passports could be issued Chinese passports immediately.
-- APPLE DAILY - A Shanghai-born, Hong Kong-raised Chinese female accountant could become the first Chinese to sit in the Australian Parliament.
-- ORIENTAL DAILY NEWS - British tabloid The Sun published video pictures showing Princess Diana meeting her horse-riding coach and lover in secret.

-- More than 300 companies in Hong Kong are involved in the birds' nest business. In recent years, the production of the Chinese delicacy has moved to southern China. As living standards rise, eating birds' nest soup has become popular in China.
-- SING TAO DAILY - Beijing police have detained Chinese dissident Liu Xiaobo and ransacked his home. Another dissident, Wang Xizhe, was followed by policemen.
-- HONG KONG ECONOMIC JOURNAL - The Hong Kong Stock Exchange had prepared a plan to cut transaction costs, which would be presented to the financial secretary before the end of the month.

-- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST - A study by China's State Information Centre proposed lowering the ratio of reserve deposits mainland banks must keep with the central bank to take effect by the last quarter of the year, followed by a third cut in lending rates.

-- HONGKONG STANDARD - Chinese Vice-Premier Li Lanqing received a major boost in his bid for a higher position in the Communist Party hierarchy after being given a fresh portfolio to oversee foreign affairs.

-- Talks between Hongkong Telecom and the government about the possible early termination of the phone company's international calls monopoly were believed to be deadlocked because of their disagreement over the amount of compensation.
